raw_text:
- The objective of this study is to explore the underlying reasons for persistently varying completion times among sites employing the same nominal work process.
- The scope encompasses an analysis of measurable factors that contribute to these completion-time differences and the identification of observational cues that can differentiate competing explanations.

Assumptions
- It is assumed that completion times differ across sites despite using identical nominal work processes.
- It is assumed that measurable factors are present which can account for these differences, such as human behavior, resource allocation, or environmental conditions.

Research design
- This study adopts a software-testing methodological approach, utilizing a cross-sectional design to gather data from multiple sites in parallel.
- A comparative case study methodology will be employed to systematically observe and compare the performance of various sites implementing the same nominal work process.

Data or evidence needed
- Data collection includes empirical observations, process documentation, and performance metrics such as completion times, resource utilization, and utilization rates.
- Qualitative data, such as participant interviews and direct observation, will provide insights into operational practices and workarounds.
- Secondary data, such as industry benchmarks and academic standards, will help establish baselines and identify potential influencing factors.

Measurement
- Completion times will be measured using standardized timekeeping methods to ensure consistency across sites.
- Resource utilization will be quantified through direct measurement or standardized proxies.
- Utilization rates will be calculated from process documentation and observed workflows.

Analysis
- An analysis of variance (ANOVA) will be employed to assess the statistical significance of differences in completion times across sites.
- Regression analysis will identify which measurable factors most significantly influence completion times.
- Inferential statistics will help to validate causal relationships and distinguish between competing explanations.

Decision / stopping rule
- The study will continue until data saturation is achieved, indicated by consistent findings across multiple sites and minimal new insights gained from additional observations.
- Decision to conclude will be reached when we reach a point of theoretical saturation or meet predefined sample size targets.

Limitations
- Potential limitations include the possibility of observer bias during data collection and inherent challenges in accurately measuring some factors.
- The external validity of the findings may be questioned, given the specific context of the sites studied.
- The results may be generalized to other sites with similar nominal processes, but the applicability could vary depending on the industry or specific operational context.
